records.name: French Polynesia
records.summary_text: French equality law applies in full — gender-identity anti-discrimination protections since 2012, hate-crime provisions since 2017, a conversion-practice ban since 2022, and legal gender recognition without medical prerequisites — and it lands on genuinely entrenched indigenous ground: the mahuu third-gender role predates colonisation, rae-rae identities are visible in daily life across the archipelago, the territory hosted its first international LGBTQIA+ rights colloquium in 2023 with government and church participation, and travel literature calls the openness cultural rather than legal.

records.name: Faroe Islands
records.summary_text:
A self-governing archipelago in the Realm of Denmark: domestic equality and family law are set locally, beneath a Danish human-rights framework. Same-sex marriage arrived only in 2017, late for the Nordics, after church-state friction. Nothing in the audited record criminalises trans people or documents enforcement against them.

records.name: Greenland
records.summary_text:
A self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark, with its own parliament and courts for domestic law. Its LGBT record is quiet and consensual: partnership law came from the Danish model in 1996 with virtually no debate; marriage equality was adopted from Danish legislation in 2016, passed unanimously by the local parliament with the established church's bishop supportive; and in 2016 the territory took a self-declaration approach to gender recognition, ahead of the metropole's own practice.
